extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, and colonial patent office administrators seeking guidance on obtaining and enforcing patents in British colonies (late 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive requirements for applying for, prosecuting, maintaining, and enforcing letters patent across various British colonies (filing, specification content, novelty, term, fees, working requirements, remedies). Useful for preparing applications and complying with colonial patent laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a complete specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person desirous of obtaining letters patent must file a complete specification in the office of the Registrar/Colonial Secretary (in duplicate where required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must clearly describe the invention and state clearly what is claimed as new; must be in writing and usually signed by the applicant or agent. Drawings are to be furnished where necessary; some jurisdictions require duplicate copies and permit inspection of specifications in public offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration / oath of inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must make oath or declaration that he is the inventor (or that he believes the deceased applicant was the inventor) and must sign the application papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor is dead, the applicant (assignee or legal representative) must state belief and domicile; power of attorney or stamped proofs may be required in some colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement (not previously known or used)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be new; patents will be refused or held void when the invention is already in possession of the public, previously described in a printed publication, or previously patented in the colony or elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several jurisdictions specify that public use, prior publication, or earlier foreign patents defeat novelty; examples: Commissioner may refuse if 'there is no novelty' or 'described in a printed book.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be of utility or have practical use; inventions of 'no utility' may be refused or patents revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple colonies (e.g., India, Fiji) list 'of no utility' as a ground for refusing or revoking an exclusive privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: First and true inventor / entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted to the first and true inventor; applications where applicant is not the inventor may be refused or the privilege vested in the actual inventor by court order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the actual inventor proves fraud, courts may vest the exclusive privilege in the actual inventor and require repayment of profits to him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficiency and particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must particularly describe and define the nature of the invention and the manner of performing it, distinguishing explicitly between what is old and what is new where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient or defective specifications may be amended; patents may be surrendered and new patents issued with amended specifications where description is insufficient or claims overbroad if errors arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and models requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are to be furnished where necessary and a working model or specimens may be required unless dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some offices require drawings in duplicate; models or specimens must be sufficient for experiments; authorities may demand a model at applicant's cost (e.g., India).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional protection period
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional protection is granted on filing for a limited period (commonly six or twelve months depending on jurisdiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: British North Borneo provisional protection 12 months; Fiji provisional protection 6 months; Canada advertising of provisional allowance gives six months' protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for filing after foreign patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a foreign patent exists, local application must often be made within a specified period (commonly within twelve months) or rights may be affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: India, Canada, and other colonies state that local application must be made before the foreign patent has been in existence for twelve months; otherwise the exclusive privilege may be refused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of patent grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted for a specified term (commonly fourteen or fifteen years, varying by colony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Canada fifteen years; many colonies fourteen years; terms sometimes may be paid for partial durations (5, 10 years) with fees reflecting chosen term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewals / extensions of term
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents may be renewed or extended for further terms on application and payment of prescribed fees; maximum extensions vary by jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common extensions are additional seven or fourteen years on payment (e.g., Bahamas renew for further seven-year terms on payment; Commissioner may grant prolongations not exceeding fourteen years in some colonies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Working / manufacture requirement (local working)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents will be void if the construction or manufacture of the patented invention is not commenced in the colony within a specified time (commonly two or three years) and carried on continuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Barbados and Bahamas require working within three years; Canada required manufacture within two years (with possible extensions for cause); failure leads to forfeiture or may trigger compulsory licences or use orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importation exceptions and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules differ on whether importation of articles made abroad invalidates the privilege; in some colonies imported articles are permitted without invalidating the patent, in others importation after a grace period may void the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: British North Borneo/others state 'articles made abroad according to the invention can be imported without invalidating the privilege'; Canada states patents void if patentee imports articles made according to the invention into Canada within twelve months of grant (subject to extensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees, stamp duties and renewal duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Government fees are payable on sealing letters patent and at periodic intervals (commonly at years 3 and 7) or for extension; non-payment may render patents void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous colonies list specific fees (e.g., Canada: full term $60, five years $20; duties third year $50, seventh year $100; others specify £/d amounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration of assignments and licences
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents, assignments, licences, and disclaimers must be registered in the Patent Office or Registrar's office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registers of patents and proprietors are kept; failure to register may affect rights. Assignments may be local-area limited in some jurisdictions (e.g., India).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers and amendments (memorials of alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees may disclaim anything included in the patent by mistake or enter memoranda of alteration; disclaimers may require stamp duty or fees and do not affect pending suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may permit amendments; disclaimers are permitted but may not undo prior litigation effects; fees and stamp duties apply in some colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal or voiding of privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Privilege will not be granted or may be declared void for reasons including: invention not new, not patentable in law, not the true inventor, described in publication, specification insufficient, wilful or fraudulent misstatement, or invention injurious to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many colonial statutes enumerate these grounds; courts may revoke patents on proof of such defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to appeal and review (administrative recourse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may appeal adverse administrative decisions to higher authority (e.g., Governor in Council) or seek confirmation where questions of priority arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In Canada applicants may appeal to the Governor in Council; conflicting applications may be submitted to arbitrators chosen by parties and Commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for conflicting applications / priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicting applications for identical inventions are resolved by priority rules or by reference to arbitrators (one chosen by each party and a third by the Commissioner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicants apply same day, authorities may authorize both to file specifications; otherwise preference given to first applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for infringement and enforcement forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions for infringement may be tried in colonial courts (Supreme Court, Federal tribunals) with remedies including damages, injunctions, accounts, and in some cases treble damages or criminal penalties for wrongful marking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings to repeal patents may be by scire facias; particulars of breaches and objections must be given in patent actions; pleadings similar to English practice in many colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scire facias and repeal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings to repeal patents may be taken by writ of scire facias or equivalent court action, and may be issued in the colony's courts or filed where grantee is non-resident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scire facias may be filed in prothonotary office if grantee not resident; particulars of breaches and objections are to be given in patent actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking requirement for patented articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Patented articles or their packages must be stamped or marked with 'Patented' and the year of the grant; failure to mark can incur fines and wrongful marking of unpatented articles is a misdemeanor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., Canada: patentee liable to $100 fine for selling unmarked patented article; marking 'Patented' when not patented is subject to fine and imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion to restrict or preserve valid parts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification or claim is too wide causing plaintiff to fail generally but defendant is found to have infringed a properly specified part, the Court may discriminate and give judgment accordingly (i.e., preserve valid portions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may hold patent valid pro tanto for parts properly specified when overclaiming arose involuntarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use of patented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Government may use patented inventions on payment of reasonable compensation as reported by the Commissioner or settled by Governor in Council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive privilege has effect against Her Majesty but officers may use invention on agreed terms or terms settled by the Governor in Council when agreement fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection / publication of specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications are open to the public in registry offices, published in official gazettes, or in some jurisdictions inventor may request non-publication for a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bahamas/Canada open to public; Malta allows request that specification not be published and permits filing a second amended specification within a year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for exhibitions and surreptitious disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use or knowledge obtained surreptitiously or in fraud of the inventor does not defeat novelty if inventor applies within prescribed time; certified exhibitions may also be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: India explicitly protects inventors against surreptitious disclosure and certified industrial exhibitions, provided application for leave to file is within six months of commencement of such use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for unauthorised use of 'Patent' word
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be statutory penalties for unauthorised use of the word 'Patent' or wrongful marking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cape of Good Hope and other colonies impose monetary penalties (e.g., 100L or other sums) for unauthorised use of 'Patent'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local procedural forms: petition and reference to Attorney-General / Executive Council
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications commonly require a petition, specification, declaration, and a reference to the Attorney-General or Executive Council whose certificate or advice leads to grant or refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Attorney-General often issues certificate of allowance; Governor or Executive Council may grant or refuse patents based on that advice (procedures closely modelled on British Patent Law Amendment Act 1852 in many colonies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender and separate patents for distinct parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees may surrender existing patents and obtain separate patents for distinct and separate parts of the invention where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and Patent Offices may issue separate patents when correction or segregation of claims is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local limitation of rights and assignment geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments may be made for any local area and patents may be issued to assignees of persons who obtained patents elsewhere; local scope of assignment may be statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: India and other colonies allow assignments for local areas; extension of foreign patents to colonies possible under local ordinances.
